quote: es schon eine sehr schwierige Aufgabe ist, bloss zu beweisen, dass unsere Differentialg. [-diese-] durch [-e-] bloss eine Quadratur nicht lösbar ist
english: it is already a very difficult task merely to prove that our differential equation is not solvable by just one quadrature
topic: The page discusses how hard it is to prove that a differential equation cannot be solved by a single quadrature, then asks how solids, liquids, gases, aether and electricity should be described under molecular theory using mean values and expansions in small parameters, and finally states that the function zeta(s,x) = sum x^n/n^s satisfies no known differential equation.

triage.modern_statement: The note is a methodological remark about how hard it is to prove that something is impossible. Hilbert says it is already very hard to show that 'our differential equation' cannot be solved by a single quadrature. In modern terms: show that a given ODE has no solution of the form y = ∫R (R from the base field), or more generally no solution in a Liouvillian extension of the coefficient field. The excerpt does not say which equation 'our differential equation' is. So there is no specific problem that can be checked, only the general type of question, which belongs to differential Galois theory.
triage.answered_by: The general question, deciding when a linear ODE can be solved by quadratures, was later answered by differential Galois theory. This grew out of Picard–Vessiot theory, and Kolchin later characterised solvability by quadratures through Liouvillian extensions and the solvability of the differential Galois group. Kovacic (1986) gave a decision algorithm for second-order linear equations, and algorithms for third order also exist. The related remark on the same page, that ζ(s,x)=Σxⁿ/nˢ satisfies no algebraic differential equation, was proved by Ostrowski (1920). The sources found do not connect any of this to this specific diary note.

evidence.claim: Solving a linear differential system by quadratures (in the Liouvillian sense) is a classical problem of differential Galois theory. Solvability by quadratures means the Picard–Vessiot extension lies inside a Liouvillian extension of C(z).
Whether a system is solvable in the Liouvillian sense depends entirely on properties of its differential Galois group.
The Kovacic algorithm and its later improvements give explicit formulas for the Liouvillian solutions of second-order linear ODEs. Algorithms for third order also exist.
Kovacic (1986) classified the possible differential Galois groups of second-order equations, which makes deciding Liouvillian solvability possible.

Ostrowski proved Hilbert's conjecture that ζ(x,s)=Σxⁿ/nˢ cannot be written as a composition of one-variable analytic functions and algebraic functions; the Ostrowski biography also credits him with showing it satisfies no algebraic partial differential equation.
Hilbert raised this question about the Lerch zeta function in his 1900 problem list. Ostrowski's result was seen as partly answering a Hilbert problem.

triage.why: The fragment refers to an unnamed 'our differential equation' and treats the difficulty of proving it cannot be solved by a quadrature as an example. It does not state a specific problem, so the exact equation cannot be identified or its fate traced. The general kind of question (deciding solvability by quadratures) was later settled systematically by differential Galois theory, and that area is still worked on, especially through algorithms. This is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems. The ζ(s,x) remark on the same page does match Hilbert's 1900 lecture and was settled by Ostrowski in 1920, but that is a separate note.
